theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Ohm's Law and Resistance

Ohm's law has a microscopic form that explains where resistance comes from. Inside a conductor an electric field E drives a current density J (current per unit area), and for an ohmic material the two are proportional, J = σE. For a uniform wire of length l and area A the field is E = V/l and the current is I = JA, so I = σAV/l. Rearranged this is V = I × l/(σA), which is exactly V = IR with R = ρl/A. Resistance is therefore just conductivity scaled by the wire's geometry.

theoryAdd.plainText: J = I/A = σE, so R = l/(σA) = ρl/A

theoryAdd.text: For a non-ohmic device the ratio V/I changes from point to point on its characteristic. The value of V/I at a chosen operating point is called the static or DC resistance, while the slope ΔV/ΔI of the curve at that point is the dynamic or AC resistance. For an ohmic resistor the two are equal and constant; for a forward-biased diode the dynamic resistance is much smaller than the static value.

rows: Stretched to n times length (same volume)
Cut into n equal parts joined in parallel
each part R/n, n in parallel
Same material and mass, length × n

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 1 - resistance of a line at working temperature
Aluminium wire: l = 2 km, d = 3 mm, rho(20 C) = 2.8e-8 ohm-m, alpha20 = 0.0039 /C
Step 1: A = pi d^2 / 4 = pi x (3e-3)^2 / 4 = 7.069e-6 m^2
Step 2: R20 = rho l / A = 2.8e-8 x 2000 / 7.069e-6 = 7.92 ohm
Step 3: R50 = R20 [1 + alpha20 (50 - 20)] = 7.92 x 1.117 = 8.85 ohm
Step 4: current from a 24 V source at 50 C: I = 24 / 8.85 = 2.71 A
Check: forgetting the /4 in the area would give R 4 times too small.

Because the resistance of a pure metal falls almost linearly as it is cooled, the straight line extended backwards meets zero resistance at a temperature −T, where T = 1/α₀. For copper T ≈ 234.5 °C. The resistances at any two temperatures are then in the ratio of their distances from −T, which avoids having to convert α from one reference temperature to another.

theoryAdd.plainText: R₂/R₁ = (T + t₂)/(T + t₁), T = 1/α₀ ≈ 234.5 for copper

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 2 - finding temperature from resistance
A copper coil measures 30 ohm at 15 C and 35 ohm after running. alpha0 = 0.00427 /C
Step 1: R0 = R15 / (1 + alpha0 x 15) = 30 / 1.06405 = 28.19 ohm
Step 2: Rt = R0 (1 + alpha0 t)  ->  t = (Rt/R0 - 1) / alpha0
Step 3: t = (35 / 28.19 - 1) / 0.00427 = 0.2414 / 0.00427 = 56.5 C
Cross-check with T = 1/alpha0 = 234.2: t2 = (35/30)(234.2 + 15) - 234.2 = 56.5 C
Temperature rise = 56.5 - 15 = 41.5 C

A series combination of a positive-coefficient conductor and a negative-coefficient one can be made almost temperature independent. The change in total resistance for a small temperature rise Δt is (R₁α₁ + R₂α₂)Δt, so it vanishes when R₁α₁ = −R₂α₂. For example, 2 Ω of copper (α ≈ 0.0043/°C) needs 2 × 0.0043/0.0005 = 17.2 Ω of carbon (α ≈ −0.0005/°C) in series.

items: Using the diameter in place of the radius in A = πr², which makes the area four times too large.
Leaving the area in mm² or cm² instead of converting to m² (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m²).
Applying α₀ to a resistance measured at 20 °C; use α₂₀, the two-temperature formula or first find R₀.
Treating resistivity as if it depended on the length or area of the sample; it depends only on the material and its temperature.
Assuming a stretched wire only gets longer; at constant volume its area falls too, so R rises as the square of the stretch.

theoryAdd.text: For stretch, cut-and-parallel and same-mass questions, work with ratios rather than actual values: write R ∝ l/A, express the new l and A as multiples of the old, and the answer usually drops out as n or n².

questions.questionText: A heating element of resistance 46 Ω is connected to a 230 V supply. The current it draws is:
A current of 2.5 mA flows through a 4.7 kΩ resistor. The voltage across the resistor is:
On the V-I graph of an ohmic conductor, with voltage V on the vertical axis and current I on the horizontal axis, the slope of the straight line represents:
questions.explanation: Slope = ΔV/ΔI = R. If the axes were swapped (I vertical) the slope would be the conductance 1/R.

questions.questionText: Ohm's law cannot be applied directly to which of the following?
options: A copper wire at constant temperature
questions.explanation: A diode is non-linear and unilateral: its V/I ratio changes with the applied voltage and with polarity, so it is non-ohmic. The others are ohmic conductors.

questions.questionText: The SI unit of resistivity is:
questions.explanation: From ρ = RA/l the unit is Ω × m²/m = Ω·m. S/m is the unit of conductivity, the reciprocal of resistivity.

questions.questionText: For a metal wire kept at constant temperature, which of the following does NOT change its resistance?
options: The material it is made of
questions.explanation: R = ρl/A depends on material (ρ), length and area. For an ohmic conductor the current simply changes in proportion to the voltage, so V/I stays the same.

questions.questionText: The conductance of a 25 Ω resistor is:
The SI unit of conductivity σ is:
questions.explanation: σ = 1/ρ, so its unit is 1/(Ω·m) = S/m. The siemens alone is the unit of conductance.

questions.questionText: When the temperature of a pure metal conductor rises, its resistance:
questions.explanation: Pure metals have a positive temperature coefficient: stronger lattice vibration scatters the free electrons more, so resistance rises.

questions.questionText: Which material is most suitable for precision standard resistors because its resistance hardly changes with temperature?
questions.explanation: Manganin (a copper-manganese-nickel alloy) has a temperature coefficient close to zero. Copper and tungsten have large positive coefficients and carbon has a negative one.

questions.questionText: An open circuit between two points has:
options: Zero resistance and zero voltage across it
Zero resistance and a very large current
Infinite resistance and zero current through it
Infinite resistance and maximum current through it
questions.explanation: An open circuit is a break in the path: R → ∞, so I = V/R = 0 even though a voltage may appear across the gap. Zero resistance describes a short circuit.

questions.questionText: The diameter of a wire is doubled while its length and material stay the same. Its new resistance, in terms of the original resistance R, is:
questions.explanation: A = πd²/4, so doubling d makes the area four times larger and R = ρl/A becomes one-quarter.

questions.questionText: Ohm's law, V ∝ I, holds for a metallic conductor provided that:
options: Its temperature and other physical conditions remain constant
The conductor is made of an alloy
questions.explanation: The proportionality between V and I holds only while the physical state, chiefly the temperature, of the conductor is unchanged.

questions.questionText: A resistor draws 2 A from a 12 V supply. If the supply is raised to 18 V and the resistance stays the same, the current becomes:
questions.explanation: R = 12/2 = 6 Ω, so I = 18/6 = 3 A; the current rises in the same ratio as the voltage.

questions.questionText: A copper conductor is 100 m long with a cross-sectional area of 1 mm². Taking ρ = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, its resistance is:
A nichrome wire (ρ = 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m) is 10 m long and 0.5 mm in diameter. Its resistance is approximately:
A wire of resistance 4 Ω is drawn out until its length is three times the original, its volume remaining constant. Its new resistance is:
questions.explanation: Length × 3 and area ÷ 3, so R = ρl/A rises 3 × 3 = 9 times: 4 × 9 = 36 Ω.

questions.questionText: A carbon resistor carries the colour bands yellow, violet, red and gold. The range within which its actual resistance may lie is:
questions.explanation: Yellow = 4, violet = 7, red = ×100, so the nominal value is 47 × 100 = 4.7 kΩ; gold means ±5 %, giving 4.7 kΩ ± 235 Ω = 4.465 kΩ to 4.935 kΩ. The first option wrongly uses ±10 % (silver).

questions.questionText: Two wires of the same material and length have diameters in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of their resistances R₁ : R₂ is:
questions.explanation: R ∝ 1/A ∝ 1/d², so R₁/R₂ = (d₂/d₁)² = 2² = 4, i.e. 4 : 1.

questions.questionText: Two wires are made from the same material and have equal mass. Their lengths are in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of their resistances R₁ : R₂ is:
questions.explanation: For fixed mass (fixed volume) A = volume/l, so R = ρl/A = ρl²/volume ∝ l². R₁/R₂ = (1/2)² = 1/4.

questions.questionText: A copper tube 2 m long has an outer diameter of 10 mm and an inner diameter of 8 mm. Taking ρ = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, its resistance from end to end is about:
questions.explanation: Only the metal ring carries current: A = π(D² − d²)/4 = π(100 − 64)/4 = 28.3 mm², so R = ρl/A = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ × 2/(28.3 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 1.22 mΩ. Using the outer or inner circle alone gives 0.438 mΩ or 0.684 mΩ.

questions.questionText: The temperature coefficient of resistance of a metal at 0 °C is 0.004 /°C. Assuming it stays constant, at what temperature will the resistance of the metal be double its value at 0 °C?
A copper winding has a resistance of 10 Ω at 25 °C. Using the inferred zero-resistance temperature of copper, −234.5 °C, its resistance at 75 °C is:
Which of the following statements about resistivity is NOT correct?
options: It is a property of the material of the conductor
Its SI unit is the ohm-metre
It doubles when the length of the wire is doubled
For a metal it increases as the temperature rises
questions.explanation: Resistivity is a material constant at a given temperature; doubling the length doubles the resistance R, not the resistivity ρ.

questions.questionText: The resistance of carbon or a pure semiconductor falls as its temperature rises mainly because:
options: More charge carriers are freed, and this outweighs the increased scattering
The material expands and its area increases
The free electrons stop colliding with the lattice
questions.explanation: Heating breaks more covalent bonds, so the carrier concentration rises steeply; this effect dominates the extra lattice scattering, giving a negative temperature coefficient.

questions.questionText: The resistance of a metallic conductor increases with temperature because:
options: The number of free electrons falls sharply
The conductor contracts and its area decreases
The charge on each electron increases
Stronger lattice vibrations scatter the free electrons more often
questions.explanation: In a metal the free-electron density is practically fixed; heating increases the vibration of the lattice ions, which shortens the time between collisions and reduces the drift for a given field.

questions.questionText: A copper conductor (σ = 5.8 × 10⁷ S/m) carries a uniform electric field of 0.01 V/m. The current density in it is:
questions.explanation: Microscopic Ohm's law: J = σE = 5.8 × 10⁷ × 0.01 = 5.8 × 10⁵ A/m².

questions.questionText: A conductor with a cross-sectional area of 2.5 mm² carries a current of 10 A. The current density is:
The resistance of a tungsten filament lamp measured cold with an ohmmeter, compared with the value V²/P calculated from its rating, is:
questions.explanation: Tungsten has a large positive temperature coefficient; the filament runs at about 2500 °C, so its hot resistance is roughly 10 to 15 times the cold value. This is why a lamp draws a surge of current when switched on.

questions.questionText: For a non-linear device, the ratio V/I at a particular operating point on its characteristic is called its:
questions.explanation: V/I at a point is the static resistance; the slope ΔV/ΔI at that point is the dynamic resistance. The two are equal only for an ohmic element.

questions.questionText: Three resistors with conductances 0.2 S, 0.05 S and 0.25 S are connected in parallel across a 10 V supply. The total current drawn is:
questions.explanation: Parallel conductances add: G = 0.2 + 0.05 + 0.25 = 0.5 S, so I = GV = 0.5 × 10 = 5 A.

questions.questionText: A wire 2 m long with a cross-sectional area of 1 mm² has a resistance of 0.04 Ω. The conductivity of its material is:
A wire is stretched so that its length increases by 10%, its volume remaining constant. Its resistance increases by:
questions.explanation: Length × 1.1 and area ÷ 1.1, so R × 1.1² = 1.21, an increase of 21%.

questions.questionText: The resistance of a circuit increases by 25% while the applied voltage is kept constant. The current decreases by:
questions.explanation: I ∝ 1/R, so I_new = I/1.25 = 0.8I; the current falls by 20%, not 25%.

questions.questionText: Wires A and B are made of the same material. A is twice as long as B and has three times the diameter of B. The ratio R_A/R_B is:
Which of the following statements about conductance is NOT correct?
options: Conductances connected in series add directly
Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance
Its SI unit is the siemens, formerly the mho
Conductances connected in parallel add directly
questions.explanation: In parallel, G_total = G₁ + G₂ + …; in series it is the resistances that add, so 1/G_total = 1/G₁ + 1/G₂ + ….

questions.questionText: A copper wire is 500 m long and 2 mm in diameter. Taking ρ = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m at 20 °C and α₂₀ = 0.00393 /°C, its resistance at 60 °C is approximately:
A coil has a resistance of 20 Ω at 20 °C and 24 Ω at 70 °C. Its temperature coefficient of resistance referred to 0 °C (α₀) is approximately:
questions.explanation: 20 = R₀(1 + 20α₀) and 24 = R₀(1 + 70α₀). Dividing: 24 + 480α₀ = 20 + 1400α₀, so α₀ = 4/920 ≈ 0.00435 /°C (the value 0.004 is α₂₀, not α₀).

questions.questionText: The field winding of a machine has a resistance of 40 Ω at 20 °C. After a long run its resistance is 48 Ω. Taking α₂₀ = 0.00393 /°C for copper, the final temperature of the winding is approximately:

A 1 Ω copper resistor (α = +0.004 /°C) is to be connected in series with a carbon resistor (α = −0.0005 /°C) so that the total resistance does not change with small temperature changes. The carbon resistor should be:
questions.explanation: Zero net change requires R_Cu α_Cu = R_C |α_C|: 1 × 0.004 = R_C × 0.0005, so R_C = 8 Ω.

questions.questionText: A tungsten lamp filament has a resistance of 20 Ω at 20 °C. When lit it draws 0.5 A from a 120 V supply. Taking α₂₀ = 0.005 /°C and assuming it stays constant, the filament temperature is approximately:
A copper wire 1000 m long has a mass of 8.9 kg. Taking the density of copper as 8900 kg/m³ and ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, the resistance of the wire is:

A copper coil connected to a 110 V DC supply draws 5 A when switched on at a room temperature of 15 °C. After some hours the current has fallen to 4.4 A. Taking α₀ = 0.00427 /°C, the final temperature of the coil is approximately:
When the voltage across a fixed resistor is increased by 20 V, the current through it increases by 25%. The original voltage across the resistor was:
questions.explanation: R is constant, so V/I = (V + 20)/(1.25I) gives 1.25V = V + 20, so V = 80 V.

questions.questionText: A rectangular metal block measures 1 cm × 2 cm × 4 cm. The ratio of the largest to the smallest resistance that can be measured between a pair of opposite faces is:
questions.explanation: R_max = ρ(4)/(1 × 2) = 2ρ and R_min = ρ(1)/(2 × 4) = ρ/8 (lengths in cm), so the ratio is 2/(1/8) = 16.

questions.questionText: A load 50 m away from a supply is fed by a two-core copper cable, each core having a cross-section of 6 mm² (ρ = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m). When the load draws 20 A, the total voltage drop in the cable is approximately:
questions.explanation: The current flows out and back, so l = 100 m: R = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ × 100 / 6 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.287 Ω; drop = IR = 20 × 0.287 ≈ 5.73 V.
